content: Glycosuria, also known as glucosuria, is a condition characterized by the abnormal excretion of glucose in the urine due to osmotic diuresis. This occurs when the kidneys fail to reabsorb glucose from the plasma, leading to its presence in the urine. The most common cause of glycosuria is untreated diabetes mellitus. When plasma glucose levels exceed the renal threshold for glucose reabsorption, the proximal tubules of the kidneys are unable to reabsorb the excess glucose, which is then excreted in the urine. The high osmolarity of glucose in the urine draws water into the urine, resulting in increased urine volume, a hallmark symptom of glycosuria. Glycosuria can occur as a physiological response to elevated blood glucose levels, such as in alimentary glycosuria, or as a pathological condition. In cases where glycosuria occurs despite normal plasma glucose levels due to a reduced renal threshold for glucose reabsorption, it is referred to as renal glycosuria. Interestingly, glycosuria has been explored as a therapeutic mechanism in diabetes mellitus, as inducing glycosuria can improve glycemic control and reduce cardiovascular risks in diabetic patients. Causes of Glycosuria The primary conditions associated with glycosuria include diabetes mellitus and pregnancy. Certain medications, such as chlorpromazine, cidofovir, hydrochlorothiazide, prednisolone, streptozocin, ACE inhibitors (e.g., captopril, enalapril), and SGLT2 inhibitors, can also induce glycosuria. Historical Perspective Glycosuria was first identified in 1889 by von Mering and Minkowski. Classification Glycosuria can be classified into several types: Alimentary glycosuria Renal glycosuria Diabetic glycosuria Iatrogenic glycosuria (caused by medical treatment) Glycosuria associated with syndromes or diseases, such as Fanconi syndrome or Wilson disease Pathophysiology The development of glycosuria is driven by either elevated plasma glucose levels or a reduced threshold for glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubules of the kidneys. Genetic mutations, such as those in the SLC5A2 and HNF1A genes, can contribute to the pathogenesis of renal glycosuria. Typically, when plasma glucose levels exceed 180 mg/dL, the kidneys are unable to reabsorb the excess glucose, leading to its excretion in the urine. However, the renal threshold for glucose reabsorption varies among individuals and changes with age. Clinical Features The simultaneous excretion of glucose and water in the urine results in symptoms such as: Polyuria (excessive urination) Polydipsia (excessive thirst) Differentiating Glycosuria from Other Conditions When glucose is detected in the urine, differential diagnoses should include: Diabetes mellitus Renal glycosuria Alimentary glycosuria Fanconi syndrome (characterized by the presence of glucose and other solutes in the urine) Wilson disease The underlying cause of glycosuria can be determined based on clinical and laboratory findings. Epidemiology and Demographics The global prevalence of glycosuria is estimated to be 3,000–5,000 cases per 100,000 individuals. The incidence of glycosuria is increasing due to the rising prevalence of diabetes mellitus and the use of medications like SGLT2 inhibitors, which promote glycosuria to improve glycemic control. Glycosuria can occur in individuals of all age groups, but its prevalence increases with age due to a decline in the renal threshold for glucose reabsorption. While glycosuria affects both men and women, it is slightly more common in males. There is no significant racial predisposition to glycosuria. Risk Factors Risk factors for glycosuria include: Common complications include persistent polyuria, polydipsia, and mild growth retardation. The severity of glycosuria tends to increase with age due to a declining renal threshold for glucose reabsorption. Despite these complications, the prognosis for glycosuria is generally excellent, with no reported cases of mortality directly attributable to the condition. Diagnosis The diagnosis of glycosuria depends on its underlying cause: Renal glycosuria: Characterized by the presence of glucose in the urine despite normal blood glucose levels, normal glycosylated hemoglobin, and normal free fatty acid levels. Glycosuria in this case is independent of carbohydrate intake and is not associated with diabetic symptoms. Alimentary glycosuria: Diagnosed when fasting blood glucose levels are normal, but postprandial blood glucose levels exceed 180 mg/dL. Diabetic glycosuria: Diagnosed in the context of known diabetes mellitus. Symptoms Symptoms of glycosuria may include: Polyuria Polydipsia Weight loss Physical Examination Patients with glycosuria typically appear normal during physical examination. However, in specific conditions such as pregnancy or starvation, patients may exhibit signs of dehydration or ketosis. Laboratory Findings Laboratory tests reveal the presence of glucose in the urine. Blood glucose levels may or may not be elevated, depending on the underlying cause of glycosuria. In some cases, other solutes may also be detected in the urine, depending on the pathophysiology. Other Diagnostic Studies Additional diagnostic studies include microscopic urine analysis and the use of glucose oxidase reagent strips to confirm the presence of glucose in the urine. Treatment The primary treatment for glycosuria involves achieving tight glycemic control in cases of diabetes mellitus. A high-protein diet may help reduce the proportion of glucose in the diet and subsequently decrease glucose excretion in the urine.
